blocks.text: Seneca, De Beneficiis book 2, ch. 29: They complain that dogs surpass us in keenness of scent, and eagles in sharpness of sight. Apuleius, Florida book 1: If they were stronger in the judgement of the eyes than of the mind, then surely wisdom would have to be conceded to the eagle. Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 7: It is said to have such power of vision that, when it is borne over the seas on motionless wing and is not visible to human eyes, it sees little fish swimming from so great a height. Sidonius, book 7, Letter 14: But perhaps they prefer the power of seeing: as though the sight of eagles were not more eminent. Philes, ch. 1:
Πλὴν ὀξυδερκής ἐστιν ὁ πτηνοκράτωρ, Καὶ μέχρι σητὸς ἐκ νεφῶν πάντα βλέπει· [Plēn oxyderkēs estin ho ptēnokratōr, Kai mechri sētos ek nephōn panta blepei]

But the prince of birds is sharp-sighted (that is, the eagle), and from the clouds sees everything, down to a moth. Apostolius, Adage 62: Ὀξύτατα ὁρᾷ ἐκ πολλοῦ τοῦ αἰθέρος [Oxytata hora ek pollou tou aitheros]. And among the Arabs, Damir, though not without hyperbole: وهو حاد البصر يري الجيفة من اربع ماية فرسخ [wa-huwa ḥādd al-baṣar yarī al-jīfa min arbaʿ māya farsakh] It is of the keenest sight, so that it sees a carcass from four hundred parasangs. To this many refer the name aquila, as if it were said from the sharpness [acumen] of sight. Accordingly it alone of animals is said to gaze at the sun with unblinking eyes, and not to regard its chicks as genuine unless they endure the light of the sun.

There follows in Job: And its chicks suck up blood, namely from the prey which the mother carries to the nest. They suck up is in Hebrew יעלעו, by metathesis for ילועו. Since this is without parallel, some interpreters have stumbled over this word. The Greeks have φύρονται ἐν αἵματι [phyrontai en haimati], as if they had read יתגללו בדם, as in 2 Sam. XX, 12. πεφυρμένος ἐν τῷ αἵματι [pephyrmenos en tō haimati] stands for the Hebrew מתגלל בדם. This is plainly foreign to the sense. Nor do I understand what ἐστυμισμένοι [estymismenoi] in Aquila means. Be that as it may, Jerome, the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic and most of the Hebrews render it very well, and according to the mind of the sacred writer, they lick or suck up blood. You will say that the eagle is πάμπαν ἄποτον [pampan apoton], wholly without drink. For so the Philosopher asserts, History book 8, ch. 3 and 18,

[II, 757] where he charges Herodotus with ignorance, because in the siege of Nineveh he makes an eagle, presiding over an augury, drink. In the Assyrian History, that is, which is no longer extant; for in those works of Herodotus that are extant nothing of the kind is found. Hence Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 26: Οὐδέποτε αἰετὸς οὔτε πηγῆς δεῖται, οὔτε γλίχεται κονίστρας, ἀλλὰ δί- [col. 175] ψους ἀμείνων ἐστί· [Oudepote aietos oute pēgēs deitai, oute glichetai konistras, alla dipsous ameinōn esti] The eagle never needs a spring, nor does it seek to roll in the dust, but it is superior to thirst. Likewise: Ὑπερφρονῶν δὲ καὶ τῶν ὑδάτων, καὶ τῆς ἀναπαύσεως· [Hyperphronōn de kai tōn hydatōn, kai tēs anapauseōs] And it scorns both waters and rest. And Gregory of Nyssa in the book On the Soul: Πολλὰ τῶν ζώων ἐστὶ μὴ πίνοντα, ὡς ἐπί τινων ἀετῶν ἱστόρηται· [Polla tōn zōōn esti mē pinonta, hōs epi tinōn aetōn historētai] There are many animals that abstain from drink, as is related of certain eagles. Pisides in Suidas:
Ἀλλ᾽ εἰσι δίψης καὶ κρύους ἀνώτεροι, [All' eisi dipsēs kai kryous anōteroi] And they know not the force of thirst and cold.

And Suidas himself, under Γαμψώνυχος [Gampsōnychos], has this: Οἷός ἐστιν ἀετὸς, ἱέραξ, κεγχρηΐς, ἄλλα τε τὰ μὴ πίνοντα· [Hoios estin aetos, hierax, kenchrēis, alla te ta mē pinonta] Such as the eagle, the hawk, the kestrel, and other animals that do not drink. And Apostolius, Adage 62: Οὐ γὰρ ἁλίσκεται ἐν νεφέλαις ὁ ἀετὸς, καὶ δίψους ἀμείνων ἐστί. [Ou gar haliksetai en nephelais ho aetos, kai dipsous ameinōn esti] For the eagle is not caught in the clouds, nor is it overcome by thirst. But there is nothing contrary to these in Job. For he does not write that eagles drink water, but that they suck up blood; which the very authors who deny the eagle drink themselves write. Thus, on the authority of Oppian in the Ixeutica, cited by Gesner: The blood of the animals they have caught suffices them, but water they do not taste at all. As Horapollo says of the hawk: Ὕδωρ οὐ πίνει τὸ καθόλου, ἀλλ᾽ αἷμα· [Hydōr ou pinei to katholou, all' haima] It does not drink water at all, but blood. And Demetrius in the Hieracosophion: Πρῶτον μὲν τὸν φάρυγγα τοῦ ἁλόντος ὄρνιθος τέμνε, καὶ δίδου πίειν τῷ ἱέρακι θερμοῦ ἀναβλύζοντος αἵματος· [Prōton men ton pharynga tou halontos ornithos temne, kai didou piein tō hierakі thermou anablyzontos haimatos] First cut the throat of the captured bird, and give the hawk the warm, gushing blood to drink. And Aelian, History book 10, ch. 14: Σαρκῶν δὲ ἥδεται βορᾷ, καὶ πίνει αἷμα, καὶ τὰ νεόττια ἐκτρέφει· [Sarkōn de hēdetai bora, kai pinei haima, kai ta neottia ektrephei] It delights in eating flesh, and drinks blood, and with these it rears its chicks. Hesychius also, of the vulture, under Τόργιον [Torgion]: Τόργος· εἶδος γυπὸς αἱματοῤῥόφους· [Torgos; eidos gypos haimatorrophous] Torgos, a kind of vulture that sucks blood.
